newsitem.title: MALDIVES: India, Pakistan start talks full of hope.
newsitem.headline: India, Pakistan start talks full of hope.

text.p: The prime ministers of India and Pakistan began bilateral talks on Monday and Pakistani leader, Nawaz Sharif, said he hoped the negotiations would help settle long-standing differences.
"I am meeting my counterpart to find ways and means to cooperate with each other and also resolve outstanding issues," Sharif told reporters as he entered the talks at a resort in the Maldives.
Indian Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral made no comment as he entered the talks at the resort island in the Indian Ocean archipelago, 500 km (300 miles) southwest of the southern tip of India.
Earlier, he said Monday's meeting with his Pakistani counterpart would help the two nations quickly establish neighbourly relations.
India and Pakistan have fought three wars since they were carved out of British India in 1947, two of them over the Himalayan region of Kashmir.
"By grace of God our meeting this afternoon will add another milestone in this shared journey to quickly reach the destination of cooperation and good neighbourliness," the Indian leader said.

Gujral told a summit meeting of the South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation (SAARC) that he was very encouraged by Sharif's public statements and that progress in bilateral peace talks had been "wholesome".
Gujral and Sharif are joining leaders from Bangladesh, Bhutan, the Maldives, Nepal and Sri Lanka at the opening of the three-day SAARC summit on Monday.

Their discussions mark the first face-to-face meeting between the leaders of the two South Asian neighbours since April 1993, when Sharif and then Indian prime minister P.V. Narasimha Rao met on the sidelines of a SAARC conference.
It follows talks between lower-level officials in March and April this year.
Pakistani Foreign Minister Gohar Ayub Khan told reporters as he entered the talks that Pakistan would raise the issue of divided Kashmir.
Khan said the Indian army "has more or less gone berserk in occupied Jammu and Kashmir", referring to mostly Hindu India's only Moslem-majority state.

Asked what India could do to improve ties, Khan said: "Reduce the troops concentration, bring down the human rights violations, stop the gang rapes, stop burning of houses, stop extrajudicial killings."
Indian authorities deny charges of gross human rights violations in Kashmir and say that they investigate all charges of rights violation and punish army soldiers where they are found guilty.
On Monday, a strike called to protest against alleged human rights violations by Indian security forces kept shops and schools closed in Kashmir's main city, Srinagar.
The two-day strike was called by the All Parties Hurriyat (Freedom) Conference, Kashmir's leading separatist coalition that groups some 30 religious and political organisations.
Police and hospital officials say more than 20,000 people have died in a separatist revolt in India's Jammu and Kashmir state since the conflict erupted in 1990.
